assumptions: The target operator has at least one battery covered by the February 2027 passport requirement and may legally authorize an external processor in writing.
The stated onboarding and per-unit pricing are hypotheses rather than observed willingness to pay.
The founder can use AI and specialist contractors for prototype, legal, and security work, but remains constrained to five hours per day until objective traction justifies staffing.
No proprietary customer relationship, supplier data right, registry privilege, exclusive channel, or reusable cross-customer dataset exists beyond what the packet states.
Incumbents can rationally bundle upstream evidence work into their existing passport and certification offers.
evidence_needed_for_higher_score: Paid pilots from several target operators showing acquisition source and sales cycle, realized onboarding and exception hours, fully loaded contribution margin, model and unit volumes, renewal behavior, and a signed channel or workflow authorization that yields repeatable access without imposing uneconomic longevity liability.

factors.name: Core insight
factors.rationale: The February 2027 passport mandate, 71-field guidance, and documented SME data-infrastructure difficulty create a real deadline-driven evidence and systems problem. The insight correctly locates much of the work upstream in assembling and validating supplier evidence, but this need is already visible to established passport vendors and is not itself a proprietary discovery.

factors.name: Customer pain and willingness to pay
factors.rationale: Delayed market placement, rework, and unavailable or nonconforming passport records are consequential pains, and the responsible economic operator is an identifiable buyer with a mandatory outcome. Category adoption by a large battery operator supports seriousness, but there is no evidence that the proposed smaller operators will pay this entrant for the managed offer, and outsourcing does not remove their statutory responsibility.

factors.name: Business model and economics
factors.rationale: Model-onboarding fees, annual prepayment, and per-unit or minimum recurring fees could produce attractive revenue if mappings are reusable. However, realized pricing, volumes, CAC, renewal, exception labor, support, insurance, signing, hosting, backup, migration reserves, and contribution margin are all unknown; long-lived availability obligations create open-ended cost, while Minespider's fixed-price unlimited-passport plan constrains pricing power. The stated 150-account wealth path is an unsupported scenario rather than an economic case.

factors.name: Market and beachhead
factors.rationale: Covered EV, LMT, and industrial batteries define a real regulated market, and smaller operators can plausibly be underserved by enterprise implementations. Yet the proposed beachhead spans several battery and operator types, and the packet does not establish the number, concentration, accessibility, or spend of unserved Polish or regional operators, so the economically meaningful initial segment remains uncertain.

factors.name: Competitive position and domination potential
factors.rationale: Siemens, Minespider, Circulor, and a Bureau Veritas-Circulor alliance already cover creation, validation, evidence storage, traceability, integration, and implementation support. The operator controls registration and data, open standards require portability, and the venture has no customer, channel, data right, or approval gate; narrow battery expertise and service responsiveness do not presently support a dominant position.

factors.name: Expansion potential
factors.rationale: A successful workflow could extend across new models, batches, lifecycle updates, additional battery categories, and eventually other product-passport regimes. Those adjacencies are plausible, but entering them would broaden regulatory and data complexity, and generalist DPP incumbents are positioned to expand along the same path; restricted reuse of customer passport data also limits cross-customer compounding.

factors.name: Defensibility and durability
factors.rationale: The required open, interoperable, transferable architecture explicitly limits lock-in, authorized service data cannot be reused beyond service delivery, and public guidance and test environments lower schema-mapping scarcity. With nonexclusive, replaceable access and no secured relationships or rights, accumulated templates and execution learning would be useful but readily contestable.

factors.name: Strength of advantage
factors.rationale: A battery-specific, portable, hands-on service could be more approachable for a small operator than a broad enterprise suite. The packet does not show a material advantage in price, speed, completeness, trust, integration, or outcomes over incumbents that already advertise readiness checks, evidence storage, audit trails, registry integration, and guided onboarding.

factors.name: Timing and momentum
factors.rationale: The statutory start date is close, current guidance has made the data burden concrete, and documented SME implementation difficulty should concentrate attention and budgets. The still-undefined battery semantic catalogue creates implementation risk and may delay purchase decisions, but it also increases the value of preparation and expert translation during the transition.

factors.name: Distribution
factors.rationale: Testing labs, certifiers, import advisers, ERP partners, distributors, and associations are credible routes to responsible operators, and the certifier-platform partnership evidence validates the channel concept. No partner commitment, lead flow, conversion rate, sales cycle, share, or CAC is established, while scaled alliances can capture the same referrals; direct technical selling also remains necessary before a channel exists.

factors.name: Execution and risks
factors.rationale: Schema mapping, anomaly detection, and workflow automation fit the founder's data-science skills and a prototype fits the available capital. Production delivery depends on supplier cooperation and requires security, privacy, authentication, incident response, regulatory maintenance, and durable availability even after operators cease activity; this continuous burden is difficult to reconcile with a five-hour daily ceiling before staffing and validated margins.

highest_value_structural_change: Move the paid control point to a bounded supplier/model acceptance event before procurement approval, deliver portable customer-controlled evidence, and exclude continuous passport hosting unless a specialist operating partner contractually absorbs the security, migration, and longevity obligations.
main_structural_strength: A non-discretionary regulatory deadline creates an identifiable responsible buyer and recurring evidence-maintenance workflow that closely matches the founder's analytical and automation capabilities.
primary_score_limiter: The offer combines unproven small-operator economics with a replaceable, weakly defensible control point and open-ended hosting and supplier-support obligations.
strongest_disconfirming_evidence: Open standards and mandatory portability leave passport control with the economic operator, while Siemens and Minespider already offer substantially overlapping creation, validation, evidence, audit, integration, and hosting capabilities; the proposed service owns neither the regulatory gate nor an exclusive data or distribution right.
